short: The first emperor of a unified China.

short: Ancient Chinese philosopher and founder of Mohism.

short: Chinese teacher and philosopher, traditionally 551–479 BCE.
note: Kongzi, or “Master Kong,” whose teachings concern ethical cultivation, humane government, family relationships, and ritual. The Analects preserves sayings and dialogues associated with him and his disciples.

short: A pendulum that demonstrates the Earth’s rotation.
note: A freely swinging pendulum whose plane of swing changes relative to the rotating Earth. The United Nations’ gold-plated example was presented by the Netherlands in 1955.

term: Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares
short: A United Nations sculpture based on Isaiah’s image of peace.
note: Evgeniy Vuchetich’s bronze of a man hammering a sword into a farming tool, given to the United Nations by the Soviet Union in 1959. Its title echoes the biblical Book of Isaiah.

sources.label: United Nations: Let Us Beat Swords Into Ploughshares

short: The 1982 war over the Falkland Islands.
note: The conflict between Argentina and the United Kingdom after Argentine forces occupied the Falkland Islands, called the Islas Malvinas in Spanish. It ended in June 1982 with the surrender of Argentine forces.

sources.label: U.S. Department of State: South Atlantic crisis

short: An oasis on the Silk Road near the Mogao Buddhist caves.
note: An oasis town in Gansu, northwestern China, associated with the nearby Mogao cave temples and their paintings, sculptures, and extraordinary manuscript collections.

sources.label: British Library: Silk Roads exhibition guide

short: The Daoist caretaker who rediscovered Dunhuang’s Library Cave.
note: A Daoist priest caring for the Mogao caves who uncovered their sealed manuscript chamber in 1900. He later sold portions of its contents to foreign researchers including Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot.

short: The Zhou ruler traditionally associated with the Book of Changes.
note: An eleventh-century BCE Zhou ruler traditionally credited with statements interpreting the I Ching’s hexagrams. The text’s historical authorship is more complex than this traditional attribution.

short: The Chinese Communist leadership’s headquarters before Beijing.
note: A village in Hebei where the Communist Party’s central leadership was based in 1948–1949, directing the final major campaigns of the Chinese Civil War.

sources.label: China.org.cn: Xibaipo museum and historic site

short: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait of Lisa Gherardini.
note: A Renaissance portrait of Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del Giocondo, painted by Leonardo da Vinci. The painting is also known as La Gioconda and is held by the Louvre.

short: Greek philosopher and investigator of nature, 384–322 BCE.
note: A student of Plato whose writings cover logic, ethics, politics, biology, physics, and metaphysics. His explanations of nature profoundly influenced later Greek, Islamic, and European scholarship.

short: Possibly the Ming admiral who led seven great overseas expeditions.
note: Possibly Zheng He, the Chinese admiral whose fleets sailed through the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, reaching ports as far away as the east coast of Africa.

short: Hangzhou’s celebrated lake and cultural landscape.
note: A lake bordered by Hangzhou and wooded hills, shaped over centuries with causeways, islands, temples, pagodas, and gardens. Its idealized scenery profoundly influenced East Asian landscape design.

short: A Hindu scripture framed as Krishna’s counsel to Arjuna.
note: The “Song of the Lord,” a section of the Mahabharata in which Krishna addresses Arjuna’s doubts before battle. It explores duty, action, knowledge, devotion, and liberation.

sources.label: Harvard Divinity Bulletin: the Bhagavad Gita

short: The Qing dynasty’s northern modernized naval force.
note: A late-Qing naval force based partly at Liugong Island near Weihaiwei. Its defeats in the First Sino-Japanese War exposed the limits of China’s nineteenth-century military modernization.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Through Wind and Rain

short: Qing naval officer and captain of the battleship Dingyuan.
note: The captain of the Beiyang Fleet’s flagship Dingyuan during the First Sino-Japanese War. After the ship was damaged at Weihaiwei in 1895, he ordered it scuttled and took his own life.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Dingyuan

short: The 1895 battle that ended the Beiyang Fleet’s resistance.
note: A Japanese land and naval operation against the Qing naval base at Weihaiwei during the First Sino-Japanese War. Capture of the coastal forts and attacks on the ships led to the fleet’s defeat.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Weihaiwei

short: A museum preserving records of Japanese wartime suicide pilots.
note: A museum in Chiran, Kagoshima, associated with the army airbase used for special-attack missions during the Battle of Okinawa. Its collection includes pilots’ letters, photographs, and personal effects.

short: Leader of South American independence from Spain.
note: A military and political leader who helped defeat Spanish rule in northern South America and became president of the republic commonly called Gran Colombia.

short: The early republic uniting much of northern South America.
note: The republic that encompassed present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama after independence from Spain. Its union broke apart around 1830.

short: The artificial waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
note: A ship canal across the Isthmus of Panama. Locks raise vessels from sea level to an inland lake system and lower them again on the opposite coast.

short: Founder of the Mongol Empire, circa 1162–1227.
note: The Mongol ruler whose conquests established an empire that his successors extended across much of Eurasia. Its successor states included the Yuan dynasty in China and the Ilkhanate in Iran.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum: The Legacy of Genghis Khan

short: Predicting the motion of three mutually gravitating bodies.
note: The problem of finding how three bodies move under their mutual gravitational attraction. Many configurations are chaotic and require numerical methods; special exact or periodic solutions also exist.

sources.label: American Museum of Natural History: the three-body problem

short: English mathematician and physicist, 1643–1727.
note: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, developed a form of calculus, and made major discoveries in optics. His Principia appeared in 1687.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Isaac Newton

short: Mathematician and pioneer of modern computing.
note: John von Neumann, 1903–1957, made foundational contributions to mathematics, quantum theory, game theory, and computing. The stored-program computer architecture commonly named after him keeps instructions and data in memory.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: John von Neumann

short: Five special positions in a two-body orbital system.
note: Positions where a small object can remain in a fixed configuration relative to two larger orbiting bodies. L1, L2, and L3 are unstable; L4 and L5 can be stable when the larger bodies’ mass ratio is sufficiently unequal.

short: The broad region of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
note: A disk-like region beyond Neptune containing Pluto and many other icy bodies left from the Solar System’s formation. It is a major source of short-period comets.

short: A proposed distant reservoir of icy bodies around the Solar System.
note: A vast, roughly spherical population of icy bodies inferred from the paths of long-period comets. It is thought to extend far beyond the planets and the Kuiper Belt.

short: Quantum correlations between parts of a shared physical state.
note: A relationship in which the quantum state of a combined system cannot be described as independent states of its parts. Entanglement produces strong correlations, but cannot transmit usable information faster than light.

short: The joining of light atomic nuclei, releasing energy.
note: A nuclear reaction in which light nuclei combine into heavier ones. Fusion powers stars; energy is released when the products have less total mass than the starting particles.

short: Hydrogen with one neutron in its nucleus.
note: A stable isotope of hydrogen whose nucleus contains one proton and one neutron. It occurs naturally in water and is one of the fuels studied for fusion energy.

short: Radioactive hydrogen with two neutrons in its nucleus.
note: An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons. Fusion of tritium with deuterium produces a helium nucleus and an energetic neutron.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy: deuterium–tritium fuel

short: A doughnut-shaped magnetic device for confining hot plasma.
note: A fusion-research device that combines external magnetic fields with an electric current in the plasma to confine it within a toroidal chamber. The name comes from a Russian abbreviation.

short: The force binding quarks and holding atomic nuclei together.
note: One of the fundamental interactions, mediated by gluons between quarks. Its residual effects bind protons and neutrons into nuclei and act over extremely short distances.

short: Physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity.
note: Albert Einstein, 1879–1955, transformed ideas about space, time, gravity, and light. His explanation of the photoelectric effect earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

short: The physical theory of atomic and subatomic systems.

short: The observed growth of transistor counts on integrated circuits.

short: Physicist who led the first controlled nuclear chain reaction.

short: Astronomer and influential communicator of science, 1934–1996.

short: Relatively cool, magnetically active patches on the Sun.

short: The continuous outflow of charged particles from the Sun.

short: Yoshiki Tanaka’s Japanese space-opera series.

short: Arthur C. Clarke and Stanley Kubrick’s space-exploration story.

short: British science-fiction writer, 1917–2008.
